newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO says Bosnian Serb retaliation won't work.
newsitem.headline: NATO says Bosnian Serb retaliation won't work.

text.p: NATO supreme commander General Wesley Clark said on Friday that Serb retaliatory attacks for a raid on indicted war criminals would not intimidate the alliance-led peace force in Bosnia.

Clark made clear during a visit to Sarajevo that the alliance would not shrink form a tougher stance towards fugitives wanted for war crimes despite a wave of low-level violence in revenge for the NATO swoop.

"We've seen some efforts by some in Srpska (the Serb republic) to intimidate their own people," he told reporters. "I can tell you NATO is not going to be intimidated by any of this and we are going to follow thrrough on our own mandate."

Clark suggested that the NATO raid last week against two Serb suspects indicted by the United Nations had rattled nationalist leaders loyal to former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, himself an indicted war criminal.
"We must be having an impact on Karadzic and the rest of the war criminals there or there would not be a response," he said.
Clark met the Moslem and Croat members of Bosnia's peacetime presidency but the Serb member, hardline nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik, failed to attend.

Serb leaders have boycotted government meetings in the capital Sarajevo since last week's raid, saying NATO can no longer be trusted to provide for the security of their staff. Western mediators have dismissed the boycott as a "nonsense".
Clark also held talks with officers in the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) a week after British soldiers pounced on the two suspects in the northwest Prijedor region.

One suspect was seized and extradited to face trial before the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague and the other was shot dead resisting arrest. Both were charged under sealed indictments for leading "ethnic cleansing" against Moslems and Croats around Prijedor during the 1992-95 Bosnian war.
Bosnian Serb authorities alleged that the extradited suspect, Milan Kovacevic, had suffered a stroke while in custody and demanded his release.
Tribunal officials confirmed that Kovacevic was undergoing medical tests by Dutch doctors but declined to discuss details of his ailment.
The operation in which Kovacevic was arrested marked a shift in tactics for NATO which had previously ruled out going after suspects unless peacekeeping troops stumbled upon them.
Hours before the Clark's visit, a hand grenade detonated outside the apartment of an international police monitor in Gradiska, 50 km (30 miles) north of Banja Luka in Serb territory.
The police monitor, who was sleeping when the attack occurred, was not injured but the explosion shattered windows in his living room, U.N. officials said.

The blast, the fifth in as many days, was part of a retaliatory campaign targeting international monitors and NATO soldiers. No one has been seriously injured and Western officials said they had no plans to evacuate staff.
The explosions have been accompanied by vitriolic attacks in official Serb media against NATO and Western governments.

Diplomats said threats and minor explosions were part of an attempt by hardline nationalists loyal to Karadzic to test the resolve and unity of Western governments, which have often disagreed over how to treat the war crimes issue.
Last week's raid set off intense speculation in the local press throughout former Yugoslavia about whom the tribunal might have charged in sealed indictments and who might be arrested next.
Some Croatian newspapers alleged that Croat suspects in Bosnia would soon be snatched and charged for crimes committed against Moslem forces in central and southern Bosnia.
